comp.label: In Praise of Getting Lost
comp.compStory:
My father had a rule about maps: they stayed in the glovebox until we were properly, thoroughly lost. "Anyone can follow a line," he would say, tapping the steering wheel. "Finding your way back to one is the real skill." My mother called this rule "the scenic route". My little brother called it "the long way to the toilets".

I used to think the rule was simply stubbornness, a grown man refusing to admit that he needed help. It took me twenty years, and one very wet afternoon in the Yorkshire Dales, to realise that it was something closer to a gift.

I was eleven that summer and my brother was eight. Our father had decided that we would walk from the village where we were staying to a waterfall he remembered from his own childhood. He remembered it vaguely. He remembered the path even more vaguely. After an hour, the path itself seemed to have forgotten where it was going: it thinned into a sheep track, then into a suggestion, then into nothing at all.

Panic arrived the way weather arrives in the hills: first as a grey smudge on the horizon, then all at once, soaking everything. My brother began to cry. I began to blame. Our father sat down on a rock, unwrapped a slightly squashed sandwich and asked us a question I have never forgotten.

"Which way is the wind coming from?"

At the time, it seemed the most ridiculous question a person could ask. We were lost; we were wet; we wanted answers, not a geography lesson. But he waited, chewing, until we stopped shouting long enough to feel the wind on our faces. Then he asked about the sun, which was hiding but not entirely invisible. Then about the stream we could hear but not see. Piece by piece, like a jigsaw with no picture on the box, we worked out where the village must be. Forty minutes later we walked into it, muddy and triumphant, as though we had discovered it ourselves.

We never did find the waterfall.

Today, I could not get lost in the Dales if I tried. My phone knows where I am to within a few metres. It tells me when to turn, how long the walk will take and where the nearest café is. It even warns me, politely, when it is about to rain. It is astonishingly useful, and I would not give it up. Yet I sometimes wonder what it costs.

When a blue dot does the thinking, we stop looking up. People who are told every turn often remember less of the route afterwards, which is hardly surprising: why would the brain bother to store something it can simply look up? But there is a difference between knowing where you are and knowing how you got there. The first is information. The second is understanding.

Getting lost, safely and not too often, forces us to notice things: the slope of a hill, the angle of a shadow, the sound of water. It asks us to stay calm when the answer is not handed to us. It teaches us that feeling uncertain is not the same as being in danger. These are not small lessons. Most of the important problems we will ever face do not come with a blue dot.

I am not suggesting that anyone should throw their phone into a river. (My father, for the record, now owns two.) But I do think we might occasionally leave it in our pocket, choose a direction and trust ourselves to find the way back. The worst that usually happens is a longer walk and a better story.

Last spring, I took my own daughter to the Dales. Halfway along a path that neither of us knew, she stopped and frowned at the sky.

"Which way is the wind coming from?" she asked.

I have never been prouder to be lost.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Where did the writer's father keep the maps until the family was lost?
questions.optionB: In the glovebox
questions.optionC: In his coat pocket
questions.explanation: The first sentence says the maps 'stayed in the glovebox'.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: How did the writer's opinion of the father's rule change over time?
questions.optionA: The writer has always thought it was a gift
questions.optionB: The writer has never understood why he had it
questions.optionC: The writer once saw it as stubbornness but now sees it as a gift
questions.optionD: The writer once found it funny but now finds it annoying
questions.optionE: The writer once found it useful but now thinks it is dangerous
questions.explanation: 'I used to think the rule was simply stubbornness... it was something closer to a gift.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: The path "thinned into a sheep track, then into a suggestion, then into nothing at all". What is the effect of this list?
questions.optionA: It suggests that the path was getting wider
questions.optionB: It shows the path gradually disappearing until they were completely lost
questions.optionC: It shows that the father knew exactly where he was
questions.optionD: It suggests that the walk was nearly over
questions.optionE: It shows that the sheep were blocking the path
questions.explanation: Each step in the list is fainter than the last, building up to 'nothing at all'.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "Panic arrived the way weather arrives in the hills." What does this comparison suggest about the panic?
questions.optionB: It began as a small worry and then suddenly overwhelmed them
questions.optionC: It disappeared as soon as the sun came out
questions.optionD: It was caused by a thunderstorm
questions.optionE: It stayed small and easy to ignore
questions.explanation: Like hill weather, it appears as 'a grey smudge' and then comes 'all at once, soaking everything'.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "My brother began to cry. I began to blame." What does this tell us?
questions.optionA: The brother blamed the writer for getting lost
questions.optionB: Both children blamed their father
questions.optionC: The children reacted differently: one was upset, the other looked for someone to be at fault
questions.optionD: The writer was crying because of the cold
questions.explanation: The two short sentences set the brother's tears against the writer's blaming.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why did the father ask, "Which way is the wind coming from?"
questions.optionA: Because he had forgotten his own compass
questions.optionB: Because he wanted to know whether it was going to rain
questions.optionC: To change the subject from the waterfall
questions.optionD: To give them a geography test for school
questions.optionE: To calm the children and get them to use clues to find the way themselves
questions.explanation: He waits until they stop shouting, then leads them clue by clue to work out where the village is.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "Like a jigsaw with no picture on the box". What does this suggest about how they found the way?
questions.optionA: They fitted clues together without knowing in advance what the answer would look like
questions.optionB: The map they were using was torn into pieces
questions.optionC: They had to do a jigsaw puzzle before they could leave
questions.optionD: They gave up because the task was impossible
questions.optionE: They followed a picture on a signpost
questions.explanation: Each clue (wind, sun, stream) is a piece; with no picture to copy, they had to work it out.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: How long after the father's question did the family walk into the village?
questions.optionB: About forty minutes
questions.optionC: About an hour
questions.explanation: 'Forty minutes later we walked into it.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does the writer put "We never did find the waterfall." in a paragraph on its own?
questions.optionA: To show that the father had lied about it
questions.optionB: To show, with gentle humour, that the original goal no longer mattered
questions.optionC: To explain why the family went home early
questions.optionD: To warn readers that the waterfall is dangerous
questions.optionE: To make the reader feel sorry for the brother
questions.explanation: Setting the line apart makes it stand out: the real reward was finding their way, not the waterfall.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: What is the writer's attitude to their phone?
questions.optionA: The writer refuses to use one
questions.optionB: The writer thinks phones should be banned on walks
questions.optionC: The writer finds it very useful but worries about what relying on it costs us
questions.optionD: The writer sees nothing wrong with relying on it completely
questions.optionE: The writer thinks phones are useless in the countryside
questions.explanation: 'It is astonishingly useful, and I would not give it up. Yet I sometimes wonder what it costs.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Which word is closest in meaning to "astonishingly" as it is used in the article?
questions.optionB: Slightly
questions.optionC: Unfortunately
questions.explanation: 'Astonishingly useful' means amazingly or remarkably useful.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: The writer says "there is a difference between knowing where you are and knowing how you got there". What does the writer mean?
questions.optionA: Being told your position gives you facts, but finding the way yourself builds real understanding
questions.optionB: It is impossible to know where you are without a phone
questions.optionC: Phones are more accurate than maps
questions.optionE: People should always walk the same route twice
questions.explanation: The writer explains: 'The first is information. The second is understanding.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "Most of the important problems we will ever face do not come with a blue dot." What is the writer suggesting?
questions.optionA: In life we often have to solve problems without someone showing us the answer
questions.optionB: Most problems can be solved using a phone
questions.optionC: Problems are easier to solve in the countryside
questions.optionD: People should avoid solving difficult problems
questions.optionE: Blue dots are the most important part of a map
questions.explanation: The 'blue dot' stands for being handed the answer; real problems rarely work that way.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does the writer add "(My father, for the record, now owns two.)"?
questions.optionA: To complain that the father uses his phone too much
questions.optionB: To prove that the father is very wealthy
questions.optionC: To show that the father has changed his rule about maps
questions.optionD: To explain where the writer got their own phone
questions.optionE: To add humour and show that even the writer's father is not against technology
questions.explanation: The aside is light-hearted and reassures readers that the article is not anti-phone.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does the writer say getting lost should happen "safely and not too often"?
questions.optionA: Because the writer thinks getting lost is always fun
questions.optionB: Because the writer's father insisted on it
questions.optionC: Because the writer wants people to stay at home
questions.optionD: Because getting lost is against the law
questions.optionE: To make clear the writer is not encouraging people to put themselves in real danger
questions.explanation: The qualification keeps the argument balanced: the writer values the lessons, not the risk.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: What is the main purpose of the article?
questions.optionB: To advertise a new kind of phone
questions.optionC: To warn that the Yorkshire Dales are dangerous
questions.optionD: To give directions to a waterfall in the Dales
questions.optionE: To persuade readers that finding their own way now and then is worthwhile
questions.explanation: Through a personal story and an argument, the writer encourages readers to sometimes leave the phone in their pocket.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does the article end with the writer's daughter asking about the wind?
questions.optionA: It shows that the daughter is frightened of bad weather
questions.optionB: It shows that the writer has forgotten the father's lesson
questions.optionC: It echoes the father's question, showing the lesson has been passed down
questions.optionD: It explains why they never reached the waterfall
questions.optionE: It proves that the daughter wants a phone
questions.explanation: The daughter repeats her grandfather's exact words, bringing the story full circle.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "I have never been prouder to be lost." Why is the writer proud?
questions.optionA: The writer managed to walk without a map for the first time
questions.optionB: The writer has proved the father wrong
questions.optionC: The writer has finally found the waterfall
questions.optionD: The daughter has a better phone than the writer
questions.optionE: The daughter has learned to think for herself in the same way the writer once did
questions.explanation: The daughter instinctively asks the same clue-finding question, so being lost becomes a proud moment.

questions.quest: A recipe for 4 people uses 300 g of flour. How much flour is needed for 10 people?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Solve 5x − 8 = 3x + 14.
questions.explanation: Subtract 3x: 2x − 8 = 14, so 2x = 22 and x = 11.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is the 10th term of the sequence 7, 11, 15, 19, …?
questions.explanation: It goes up by 4 each time. The 10th term is 7 + 9 × 4 = 43.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is the median of 8, 3, 11, 6, 9 and 4?
questions.explanation: In order: 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11. The middle two are 6 and 8, so the median is 7.

questions.quest: What is the area of this triangle?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A film starts at 18:45 and lasts 2 hours 25 minutes. When does it finish?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is 7.2 ÷ 0.04?
questions.explanation: Multiply both by 100: 720 ÷ 4 = 180.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 85°, 110° and 75°. What is the fourth angle?
questions.explanation: Angles in a quadrilateral add up to 360°: 360 − 85 − 110 − 75 = 90°.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: At midnight the temperature is −7 °C. By noon it has risen by 12 °C. By evening it has fallen by 9 °C. What is the evening temperature?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Pack A has 6 rolls for £2.70. Pack B has 4 rolls for £1.92. How much cheaper per roll is Pack A?
questions.optionB: 2p
questions.optionC: 3p

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is the value of the digit 7 in 3.476?
questions.optionB: 7 units
questions.optionC: 7 tens
questions.explanation: 3.476 = 3 units, 4 tenths, 7 hundredths, 6 thousandths.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A cuboid measures 6 cm by 4 cm by 2.5 cm. What is its volume?
questions.optionB: 60 cm³
questions.optionC: 98 cm³

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: How many factors does 36 have?
questions.explanation: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 36: nine factors.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Three corners of a square are at (1, 1), (5, 1) and (5, 5). Where is the fourth corner?
questions.explanation: The square has sides of 4 units; the missing corner is above (1, 1) at (1, 5).

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A car travels 150 km in 2 hours 30 minutes. What is its average speed?
questions.optionB: 65 km/h
questions.optionC: 50 km/h

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Ali is three times as old as his sister. In 4 years' time their ages will add up to 44. How old is Ali now?
questions.explanation: Sister s, Ali 3s. In 4 years: (s + 4) + (3s + 4) = 44, so 4s = 36, s = 9 and Ali is 27.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting exactly one head?
questions.explanation: The outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT. Exactly one head: HT or TH, so 2/4 = 1/2.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: In a code, PLANET is written as MIXKBQ. How would RIVER be written in the same code?
questions.optionB: PGTCP
questions.optionC: NERAN
questions.explanation: Each letter moves three places back in the alphabet: R→O, I→F, V→S, E→B, R→O.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: In a code, GOLD is written as TLOW. How would SILVER be written in the same code?
questions.optionB: RHOEVI
questions.optionC: HRLEVI
questions.explanation: Each letter is swapped with its partner from the other end of the alphabet (A↔Z, B↔Y, …): S→H, I→R, L→O, V→E, E→V, R→I.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next letter in the series: B, E, I, N, ?
questions.optionB: O
questions.optionC: R
questions.explanation: The gaps grow by one each time: +3, +4, +5, so the next is +6: N → T.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next number: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ?
questions.explanation: The differences are 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next difference is 12: 30 + 12 = 42.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next number: 1, 10, 3, 20, 5, 30, ?
questions.explanation: Two series are mixed together: 1, 3, 5, 7 and 10, 20, 30. Next comes 7.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
A four-letter word is hidden across the end of one word and the start of the next. Which pair hides it?
"Paul overslept again because his alarm failed."
questions.optionB: Paul overslept
questions.optionC: his alarm
questions.explanation: Pau(L OVE)rslept hides the word LOVE.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
A four-letter word is hidden across the end of one word and the start of the next. Which pair hides it?
"Our tea came at six."
questions.optionB: tea came
questions.optionC: at six
questions.explanation: ca(ME AT) hides the word MEAT.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word is closest in meaning to FRAGILE?
questions.optionB: heavy
questions.optionC: sturdy
questions.explanation: Fragile means easily broken: delicate.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of GENEROUS?
questions.optionB: honest
questions.optionC: wealthy
questions.explanation: Generous means happy to give; the opposite is mean.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word does NOT belong with the others?
questions.optionB: cello
questions.optionC: violin
questions.explanation: Violin, cello, harp and guitar have strings; a flute is a wind instrument.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word can go after all of these to make three new words?  foot___   sun___   star___
questions.optionB: fish
questions.optionC: ball
questions.explanation: footlight, sunlight, starlight. (Ball and step only work with foot; fish and shine only with sun and star.)

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Author is to book as composer is to ?
questions.optionB: conductor
questions.optionC: concert
questions.explanation: An author writes a book; a composer writes a symphony.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which letter completes both words?  fro (?)   (?) ate
questions.optionB: t
questions.optionC: s
questions.explanation: frog and gate. None of the other letters makes two real words.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
If these words were put in alphabetical order, which would come LAST?
stripe   strike   strife   string   stride
questions.optionB: stripe
questions.optionC: string
questions.explanation: Order: stride, strife, strike, string, stripe. The last is stripe.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Move one letter from the first word into the second to make two new words: FLIGHT   SOW. Which letter moves?
questions.optionB: I
questions.optionC: F
questions.explanation: Taking L from FLIGHT leaves FIGHT; adding it to SOW makes SLOW.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: In a code, ROPE is written as 3142 and POET is written as 4128. What does 4138 stand for?
questions.optionB: ROPE
questions.optionC: PORT
questions.explanation: From the two codes, P=4, O=1, R=3, E=2, T=8, so 4138 is PORT.

questions.subject: VERBAL

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: TEAM becomes MEAT in the same way that REAP becomes ?
questions.optionB: PARE
questions.optionC: REAP
questions.explanation: The first and last letters swap places: TEAM → MEAT, REAP → PEAR.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: If A = 2, B = 4, C = 6, D = 8 and E = 12, what is (E ÷ A) + (B − A)? Give your answer as a letter.
questions.optionB: B
questions.optionC: C
questions.explanation: E ÷ A = 6 and B − A = 2; 6 + 2 = 8, which is D.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Five friends, Ella, Jo, Mia, Raj and Sam, sit in a row. Mia sits at the left end. Jo sits next to Mia. Raj sits in the middle. Ella is not at either end. Who sits at the right end?
questions.optionB: Mia
questions.optionC: Ella
questions.explanation: From the left: Mia, Jo, Raj. Ella is not at an end, so Ella is fourth, leaving Sam at the right end.
